name: Receiver stations
source: List of VLF transmitters, Wikipedia (VLF and LF); 47 CFR 87.263 (HF air routes); ITU Radio Regulations Appendix 18 and Appendix 17 channel plans (marine VHF, HF marine); 47 CFR 95 (CB, FRS, GMRS, MURS); radioindustries.com.au (UHF CB); ETSI EN 300 401 (DAB); NOAA and WMO OSCAR (weather satellites); Wikipedia and UDXF (ACARS, VDL2); Inmarsat STD-C hobby references. Satellite navigation, Cospas-Sarsat, Iridium, Metop, FengYun, GRB, LoRa and sensors from general knowledge, not checked against a source when written.
note: Only shown with a receiver connected, and for listening only. Some countries, the UK among them, make it an offence to listen to messages not meant for you or to pass them on. Many of these are digital or encrypted, so a flag says what's there, not that you can hear it. Local things such as your own airport's frequencies aren't listed.

groups.name: VLF: naval and navigation
groups.note: A strong steady MSK signal, mostly to submarines. Encrypted: on the scope and the S meter it shows as a carrier. Below 30 kHz, on ANT1 or ANT2.

groups.name: VDL Mode 2: aircraft data
groups.note: A faster digital data link. Decoded by software, and needing more bandwidth than this mode gives: it shows on the scope.

groups.name: Weather satellites
groups.note: Digital image downlinks, decoded by software during a pass or, from geostationary orbit, all the time with a dish. NOAA-15, 18 and 19 have been decommissioned, so their 137 MHz APT is gone.

stations.label: Meteor
stations.note: Meteor-M N2-4 LRPT, 80 kbit/s. WMO OSCAR. Frequencies and modes can change with little notice

groups.name: Inmarsat
groups.note: L-band messaging from geostationary satellites. Decoded by software, with a small patch antenna.

groups.name: Distress beacons
groups.note: Emergency beacons: 406 MHz up to the satellites, and the MEOSAR downlink. Never transmit here.

groups.name: Iridium and science
groups.note: Other things worth finding on the scope.

stations.label: H line
stations.note: The hydrogen line: radio astronomy, with a dish pointed at the Milky Way

groups.name: CB: CEPT and FCC 40 channels
groups.note: Citizens Band, FM across Europe. AM and SSB are in use in the USA.

groups.name: CB: UK 27/81
groups.note: The UK's own 40 channels, FM.

groups.name: PMR446
groups.note: Licence-free handheld radios, Europe and elsewhere. Channel 1 is the usual calling channel.

groups.name: LPD433
groups.note: Licence-free low-power radios, Europe. Shares the 70 cm amateur band.

groups.name: FRS and GMRS
groups.note: United States and Canada. The same 22 channels: channels 1-7 and 15-22 are also used by GMRS, whose repeaters listen 5 MHz up.

groups.name: MURS
groups.note: United States: Multi-Use Radio Service, licence-free VHF.

groups.name: UHF CB: Australia
groups.note: Australia's 80 channel plan. 1-8 and 41-48 are repeater outputs; 31-38 and 71-78 their inputs. New Zealand's PRS is similar.

groups.name: Sensors and short range
groups.note: Remote controls, weather stations, tyre pressure sensors and LoRa. Bursts, best seen on the scope. Not private just because they're small: check the law where you are.

stations.label: ISM
stations.note: Remote controls and tyre sensors, USA

stations.label: ISM
stations.note: Remote controls, sensors, tyre pressure, Europe

stations.label: ISM
stations.note: Centre of the US 902-928 MHz ISM band

groups.name: DAB channels
groups.note: Digital radio multiplexes, 1.5 MHz wide. Band III channel centres, used mostly in Europe and Australia. The receiver can't decode DAB, but they show well on the scope.

groups.name: TV: Europe, channels 21-48
groups.note: Centre of each 8 MHz channel. Digital: seen on the scope, not listened to. Which are in use depends on the country.

groups.name: TV: USA, channels 14-36
groups.note: Centre of each 6 MHz channel. Digital: seen on the scope, not listened to.

ranges.label: OIRT FM
ranges.note: Older FM broadcast band, in parts of eastern Europe and Asia

ranges.label: Radiosondes
ranges.note: Weather balloons, which send position and readings for an hour or two after launch
